p.src: We have studied how a prescribed electromagnetic field moves a charged particle. The unfinished half of the problem is the field itself: how electric and magnetic fields evolve, and how charge and current act as their sources. Maxwell’s equations answer those questions. Before writing them, however, it is worth recovering the physical puzzle that made their relativistic structure unavoidable.

ja: 我々は、与えられた電磁場が荷電粒子をどのように動かすかを学んできた。問題の未完成な半分は場そのものである。すなわち、電場と磁場がどのように発展し、電荷と電流がどのようにそれらの源として働くかである。マクスウェル方程式がこれらの問いに答える。しかし、それを書き下す前に、その相対論的構造を不可避にした物理的パズルを思い出す価値がある。
zh: 我们已经研究了给定的电磁场如何使带电粒子运动。问题尚未完成的一半是场本身：电场和磁场如何演化，以及电荷和电流如何作为它们的源。麦克斯韦方程组回答了这些问题。然而，在写出它们之前，值得重新回顾那个使它们的相对论性结构不可避免的物理谜题。

p.src: During a visit to Belgium, a discussion of the early Solvay conferences led back to Einstein’s 1905 paper, On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies. Its first paragraph states the motivation with remarkable economy. The same electromagnetic phenomenon receives two apparently different explanations in two inertial frames. One observer calls the effect magnetic; another calls it electric. The observed motion agrees, so the two descriptions cannot represent two different pieces of physics.

ja: ベルギーへの訪問中に、初期のソルベー会議についての議論が、アインシュタインの1905年の論文運動物体の電気力学についてへと戻った。その最初の段落は、動機を驚くほど簡潔に述べている。同じ電磁現象が、二つの慣性系で一見異なる二つの説明を受ける。一方の観測者はその効果を磁気的と呼び、他方は電気的と呼ぶ。観測される運動は一致するので、二つの記述は物理学の異なる二つの部分を表すことはできない。
zh: 在访问比利时期间，一场关于早期索尔维会议的讨论引回到了爱因斯坦1905年的论文《论动体的电动力学》。它的第一段以非凡的简洁陈述了动机。同一个电磁现象在两个惯性系中得到两种表面上不同的解释。一个观察者称该效应为磁的；另一个称它为电的。所观察到的运动一致，因此这两种描述不可能代表两块不同的物理。

p.src:
Now keep the wire, or the test charge, fixed and move the magnet instead. The changing magnetic configuration produces an electromotive force, which in local language is an electric field. That electric field pushes the stationary charge in the same transverse direction. Thus the two descriptions are $\begin{aligned}\text{moving charge, fixed magnet:}\quad&
q\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B,
\\
\text{fixed charge, moving magnet:}\quad&
q\,\mathbf E'.\end{aligned}$ The relative motion is the same. A theory of relativity must therefore explain how a field that is purely magnetic in one frame acquires an electric component in another.

Equation [eq:f-boost-law] gives $\begin{aligned}F'^{0z}
&=
\Lambda^0{}_\sigma
\Lambda^z{}_\tau F^{\sigma\tau}
\\
&=
\Lambda^0{}_x\Lambda^z{}_zF^{xz}
\\

(-\gamma v)(1)(-B_y)
=
\gamma vB_y.\end{aligned}$ Since $F'^{0z}=-E'_z$ in this convention, $E'_z=-\gamma vB_y.$ The sign depends on the declared axis and field conventions; the invariant point of the calculation is $\lvert E'_z\rvert
=
\gamma\lvert vB_y\rvert
\ne0.$ The double sum collapses because the original field has only this one independent magnetic component.

In the conventions of Equation [eq:f-upper-matrix], the relevant independent component is $F^{xz}=-B_y.$ We seek the primed mixed component $F'^{0z}$, because it carries the primed $z$-component of the electric field. Equation [eq:f-boost-law] gives $\begin{aligned}F'^{0z}
&=
\Lambda^0{}_\sigma
\Lambda^z{}_\tau F^{\sigma\tau}
\\
&=
\Lambda^0{}_x\Lambda^z{}_zF^{xz}
\\
&=
(-\gamma v)(1)(-B_y)
=
\gamma vB_y.\end{aligned}$ Since $F'^{0z}=-E'_z$ in this convention, $E'_z=-\gamma vB_y.$ The sign depends on the declared axis and field conventions; the invariant point of the calculation is $\lvert E'_z\rvert
=
\gamma\lvert vB_y\rvert
\ne0.$ The double sum collapses because the original field has only this one independent magnetic component.

p.src:
For a differentiable three-vector field $\mathbf A$, $\begin{aligned}(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf A)_x
&=
\partial_yA_z-\partial_zA_y,
\\
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf A
&=
\partial_xA_x+\partial_yA_y+\partial_zA_z.\end{aligned}$ The remaining curl components follow by cyclically permuting $x\to y\to z\to x$. For a scalar field $s$, $\boldsymbol\nabla s
=
(\partial_xs,\partial_ys,\partial_zs).$ Thus a curl is a vector, a divergence is a scalar, and a gradient is a vector.

p.src: Response: In Schwarzschild coordinate time, classical infall is seen to approach the horizon asymptotically. p.src:
Equation [eq:continuity] is not an independent addition to Maxwell’s equations. Take a time derivative of Gauss’s law and a divergence of the Ampere–Maxwell law: $\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}
&=
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot
\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t},
\\
-\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J
&=
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot
(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf B)
+
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot
\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}
\\
&=
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot
\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.\end{aligned}$ The two left-hand sides are therefore equal, giving $\partial_t\rho=-\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J$, exactly Equation [eq:continuity]. What matters structurally is that the time derivative of $\mathbf E$, the displacement-current term, is essential for the divergence relation to be compatible with charge conservation.
